strengths: The manuscript addresses a relevant NLP problem: evaluating document coherence beyond comparisons with shuffled copies. Incorporating temporal covariance and covariance across embedding dimensions is a meaningful extension of the earlier BBScore. The Gaussian likelihood derivation provides a useful foundation under appropriate nonsingularity assumptions. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b04/review-experiment-gkm7l7wi/call-c0ddee01d7774187b6bec50268513dcf/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The reported improvements over the heuristic BBScore are substantial and consistent. On WikiSection, global test accuracy increases from 83.39% to 95.06% for single-sentence shuffling, and local accuracy increases from 64.06% to 74.24% for three shuffled windows.

Evaluation extends beyond artificial perturbations to human-annotated GCDC texts, encoder transfer, and human–AI comparisons. GCDC correlations exceed the readability baseline in all four domains. The appendix also reports useful optimizer, training-duration, hardware, and regularization details.
weaknesses: The BB encoder objective permits representation collapse (Section 3.2.2). Scaling encoder outputs by c and fitted covariances by c² preserves the quadratic term while driving the log-determinant contribution toward negative infinity as c approaches zero. The scale-dependent shrinkage in the main text does not prevent this. A constant encoder also minimizes the fixed-covariance quadratic training loss. The fixed ridge described in Appendix B can stabilize inversion but does not preserve information. An explicit constraint or additional objective, supported by collapse diagnostics, is needed to justify the claim that likelihood training learns meaningful Brownian-bridge representations.

The covariance used for scoring is insufficiently specified. Section 3.3 introduces an estimate for the evaluated sequence: substituting the single-sequence MLE from Theorem 2 into Theorem 3 gives BBScore = 1 whenever that estimate is invertible. When T−1 < d, this estimate is singular. Later experiments suggest reference-corpus covariance estimates, which can avoid the constant-score problem, but the paper must explicitly distinguish these procedures and specify estimation splits and inference-time regularization.

The statistical interpretation does not establish the claimed calibration. With known covariance, the proposed score follows χ²_k/k, where k=(T−1)d; it is not itself a p-value, and its variance remains length-dependent at 2/k. Replacing the true covariance with an estimate also changes the distribution in general. The tables nevertheless label the method 'P-VALUE.' Clarify the implemented statistic and validate its behavior across document lengths.

Several performance comparisons overstate the evidence. GCDC pairwise ranking accuracy cannot be directly compared with prior three-class classification accuracy. On the shared Spearman metric, the method trails the cited strongest comparator in three of four domains. Likewise, Table 2 reports local accuracy of 56.35–74.24%, versus 77.47–87.87% for Unified Coherence, contradicting the broad statement that the method matches state-of-the-art results. Different supervision requirements are relevant, but require qualified conclusions and matched comparisons.

Evidence for the BB encoder's superior transfer and distribution learning is limited. Table 4's test differences versus the CL encoder range from −3.12 to +2.10 percentage points, with no uncertainty estimates. Both transfer corpora originate from Wikipedia, and overlap checks are not described. Figure 2's qualitative trajectories do not establish agreement with the joint Brownian-bridge distribution. Quantitative distribution diagnostics and separate temporal/spatial covariance ablations would strengthen the central explanation.

The approximately 70% HC3 result supports an exploratory finding, but not the claim of competitive detection. No detector baselines are reported, and the evaluation needs clearer sample counts, pairing rules, covariance-estimation splits, and domain breakdowns. Ranking a known human–AI pair should also be distinguished from classifying an individual document.

Reproducibility remains incomplete in the manuscript: important model settings are deferred to submitted code, covariance fitting is ambiguous, and GCDC pair selection and equal-label handling are unclear. Random seeds, repeated-run variability, and validation criteria for hyperparameter selection are not reported. Together with the objective and score-definition issues, these prevent a sound Findings recommendation. The promising scoring results justify revision, with the necessary corrections and targeted experiments plausibly achievable for the next cycle.
